topic.title: The offsite is cheaper than a raise
topic.claim: The team offsite is a retention plan that costs less than a raise, and it works better than it should.
topic.moment: Two days at a resort, matching T-shirts, a trophy for 'Best Team Player'.

turn.believed: Offsites are a perk for good work.
turn.actually: A one-time trip costs less than a pay hike that compounds every year, and it buys loyalty for a few months.

topic.feeling: I had fun and I still feel a bit bought.
topic.villain: Budgets where one-time spend is easy and permanent salary is hard
topic.because: A raise sits in the cost base forever. A trip sits in one quarter, and the photos remind you of it for a year.
topic.payoff: The honest bit: the trip did make you stay. That's exactly why it was approved.
topic.behaviour: Companies fund offsites and team dinners while holding increments flat.
topic.mechanism: One-off spend buys goodwill without raising fixed costs.
topic.group: Employees at startups and mid-size companies
topic.send_to: The team group, right after the offsite photos go up
topic.why_now: Offsite season lines up with the months when increments get trimmed.

score.why: The offsite did make you stay, and that's why it was approved. It has an honest mixed feeling and is the one office pick, with a lived angle.

notes: slide 3: "And it often lands in the same months your increment gets trimmed." states a general claim about India Inc. that the sources contradict: Aon reports increments of about 9% rising to 9.1% in 2026, not trimmed. Reframe it as a typical scene the reader lives, without claiming a trend. For example: the offsite lands in the same quarter your manager says 'budgets are tight this year' and your hike comes in lower than you hoped.

Fix it to something like "Walking out on people you danced with feels worse than walking past a bigger offer." Also drop "It's not that you're naive." and say the opinion straight; the 'not X' setup reads defensive.

sources.fact: Aon projects Indian salaries will rise 9.1% in 2026, and attrition fell to 16.2% in 2025. So increments were not frozen across India Inc., and retention improved alongside them.
sources.stance: neutral: The page says nothing about offsites or trips. It credits retention to engagement, career mobility and stability, not to one-off perks in place of raises.
sources.excerpt: salaries in India will increase by 9.1 percent in 2026. / The projected 9.1 percent increase reflects a slight uptick from the actual 8.9 percent increase recorded in 2025. / overall attrition declined to 16.2 percent in 2025, returning close to pre‑COVID levels. / steady improvement in employee retention across industries.

sources.fact: Great Place To Work India found that 66% of employees contemplating leaving would accept a pay cut for better workplace conditions, and 87% of them cited culture as a key factor. Those preparing to leave were 20% to 27% less satisfied on fair pay, recognition and similar areas.
sources.stance: neutral: This partly supports the idea that non-pay factors matter for retention. It says nothing about offsites, and it lists fair pay among the sources of dissatisfaction, so it does not show a trip can replace a raise. The date is ambiguous: the page is dated 2026-08-20 and the press release is datelined 2025-12-18.
sources.excerpt: 66% of employees contemplating leaving are willing to accept a pay cut / 87% of employees thinking about leaving cited workplace culture as a key factor / Employees preparing to leave reported 20% to 27% lower satisfaction / particularly around fair pay, work-life balance, recognition, and management communication.

sources.fact: Business Today, citing Aon, reports attrition fell to 16.2% in 2025 from 17.7% in 2024 and 18.7% in 2023, with increments averaging about 9% a year. It argues that lasting retention comes more from how work is designed than from engagement programmes.
sources.stance: contradicts: The article says retention gains come less from engagement programmes than from restructuring work. That weakens the claim that a trip keeps people for a year. It also treats steady ~9% increments as part of what supports mobility.
sources.excerpt: Historically stronger salary increments averaging around 9% year-on-year

cover.headline: The team offsite is a [retention plan] cheaper than your raise
cover.sub: One gets approved in a week. The other takes a fight.

paragraphs:
The team offsite is a retention plan. It costs less than your raise.
Swipe to read →
slides.why_swipe: How can a fun trip be a retention plan?

paragraphs: Two days at a resort. Matching T-shirts, a DJ night, a trophy for Best Team Player.
Same quarter, your manager said budgets are tight this year and your hike came in smaller than you hoped.
slides.why_swipe: Why would a company pay for a trip but not a bigger hike?

paragraphs: Put the two side by side. The resort and the bus come to about ₹30,000 a head. Paid once.
slides.why_swipe: And what does the raise cost?

paragraphs: An extra 5% on a ₹12 lakh salary is ₹60,000, and next year's hike gets built on top of it. Every year.
slides.why_swipe: So what does the company actually see when it compares them?

paragraphs: Finance hates a raise because it never leaves the books. A trip is gone by next quarter.
And all it needs is a Google Form for T-shirt sizes.
slides.why_swipe: Does a two-day trip really buy anything once it's over?

paragraphs: And the trip keeps working after checkout, because the group photo becomes the team's WhatsApp DP.
So the recruiter's message a few months later feels a bit like cheating.
slides.why_swipe: Is this all just a trick, then?

paragraphs: I've worn the matching T-shirt and meant every cheer. The fun was real.
Walking out on people you danced with feels worse than walking past a bigger offer.
The trip worked. You ignored that recruiter and stayed another year.
Which is exactly why finance signed off on it.

end.save: Read it again the week your increment letter lands.
end.send: Send to the team group, right after the offsite photos go up.

draft.alt_text: An eight-slide text post arguing that company offsites work as a cheaper retention tool than raises. The offsite is two days at a resort with matching T-shirts, a DJ night and a Best Team Player trophy. It often comes in the same quarter a manager says budgets are tight and the hike comes in smaller than hoped. A one-time trip of about ₹30,000 a head costs less than a 5% raise on a ₹12 lakh salary, which is ₹60,000 and gets built on every year. Finance dislikes a raise because it stays on the books, while a trip is gone by next quarter. The photos and friendships make leaving feel like cheating. The writer admits the fun was real, and closes by saying the trip did make people stay, which is exactly why it was approved.

claims.text: An extra 5% on a ₹12 lakh salary is ₹60,000 a year (typical example)
